hero.headline: Former CIA Officer Arrested After FBI Finds $40 Million in Gold Bars at His Home
hero.body:
Federal authorities arrested David Rush, a former senior CIA officer, after FBI agents discovered approximately $40 million worth of gold bars and cash inside his Virginia home. Prosecutors allege Rush stole the assets from a CIA storage space.

Rush faces charges of theft and making false statements to federal investigators. The gold bars and millions of dollars in cash had been reported missing from his CIA storage facility before agents recovered them during a search of his residence.

The arrest marks a significant breach of trust involving a former senior intelligence official. Rush had served in a senior capacity at the CIA before the alleged theft occurred.

The FBI conducted the search that led to the discovery of the massive trove of precious metals and currency. The sheer volume of assets found inside a private residence has raised questions about how such a large-scale theft could have occurred from a secure CIA facility.

Federal prosecutors are pursuing charges related to both the alleged theft of government property and statements Rush allegedly made during the investigation. The case involves one of the largest known thefts of physical assets from a U.S. intelligence agency.

The CIA has not publicly commented on the security protocols in place at the storage facility or how the theft allegedly went undetected. The investigation into how Rush allegedly removed such a substantial quantity of gold bars from a CIA location remains ongoing.

Rush's arrest follows an FBI investigation into the missing assets. The former officer now faces federal prosecution for crimes that could result in significant prison time if convicted. The case has drawn attention to internal security measures at U.S. intelligence agencies and the safeguarding of valuable assets in their custody.

cards.headline: U.S. and Iran near deal to extend ceasefire and reopen Strait of Hormuz
cards.body:
U.S. officials say they are close to an arrangement with Iran that would extend the current ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the critical shipping lane that has been blocked during recent hostilities. President Trump has not yet approved the emerging framework, according to officials briefed on the negotiations.

The potential agreement would establish a 60-day ceasefire extension during which Iran could freely sell oil and the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened for international shipping. According to a U.S. official who spoke with Axios, talks on limiting Iran's nuclear program would also proceed during this period. As part of the arrangement, Iran would agree to clear mines it has deployed in the strait and refrain from imposing tolls on passing vessels.

In exchange, the U.S. would lift its blockade on Iranian ports that has been in effect since April 13. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the deal could achieve "a completely open" Strait of Hormuz "without tolls" if successful. The agreement would also reportedly unfreeze some Iranian assets being held in banks outside Iran.

Hostilities would be halted on all fronts, including between Israel and Lebanon. However, conflicting signals have emerged from Tehran about whether a deal has been finalized. One Iranian news agency reported that no agreement has been confirmed, highlighting the fragile nature of the diplomatic process.

The Strait of Hormuz is a vital waterway through which roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies pass. Its closure has disrupted international shipping and energy markets. Iranian media reported that the strait would remain under Iranian control, even as part of this arrangement.

Notably, a senior Iranian source told Reuters that Tehran had not agreed to hand over its highly enriched uranium stockpile. The source stated that Iran's nuclear issue was not part of the preliminary agreement. There has also been little mention in negotiations of Iran's ballistic missile program or the curbing of support for regional allies such as Hezbollah in Lebanon or the Houthis in Yemen.

Neither the U.S. nor Iran appears eager to return to full-scale conflict, despite recent military strikes exchanged between the two sides. The economic and strategic costs of continued conflict appear to be driving both sides toward a diplomatic resolution, at least temporarily.

U.S. officials stress that any final agreement requires presidential approval and that negotiations remain ongoing. The framework being discussed would need buy-in from multiple stakeholders, including regional allies and international shipping interests that depend on the strait remaining open for commercial traffic. Officials characterized the arrangement as tentative, cautioning that significant hurdles remain before a final deal can be reached.

cards.headline: Netanyahu orders Israeli military to seize 70% of Gaza Strip
cards.teaser: The Israeli prime minister directed his military to take control of most of Gaza, a move that violates the existing ceasefire agreement.
cards.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has directed the military to take control of 70 percent of the Gaza Strip, according to multiple news reports. The order appears to target Hamas by establishing Israeli control over the majority of the territory.

The directive represents a significant escalation that conflicts with the current ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas. The move threatens the stability of the existing deal and could lead to its collapse.

cards.headline: U.S. to quarantine Americans exposed to Ebola in Kenya, barring them from returning home
cards.body:
The Trump administration confirmed this week that Americans exposed to Ebola will not be permitted to return to the United States. Instead, the government is constructing a 50-bed quarantine and treatment facility in Kenya that became operational Friday.

The White House said the facility was "designed to provide access to high-quality care for Americans who would need to quickly get out of DRC and quarantine without the risks of a lengthy transport back to the US," according to a statement from a White House official.

The Kenya center will handle both quarantine for exposed individuals and treatment for those who contract the virus. The official stated the facility would provide "critical care needs, though each case will be evaluated for forward transport for more advanced care as appropriate in order to maximize patient outcomes." The official did not specify whether additional treatment would occur in the United States or Europe, where some Americans have previously received care.

The administration also did not clarify whether Americans could choose to return to the U.S. instead of going to Kenya.

The policy has drawn criticism from public health experts. Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health, said the approach raises serious concerns.

"It is shocking to me that the administration is looking to prevent Americans from coming home to receive the proven world-class care that our taxpayer-funded biocontainment and treatment units are equipped to provide," Nuzzo said. "There are profound ethical concerns with this approach."

She worried that the policy could discourage people from reporting exposures. "Without adequate plans for the safe quarantine of exposed individuals and prompt isolation of those who become infected, I fear these facilities could amplify the spread of the virus. The prospect of not being able to come home for safe and effective care may create disincentives for people to disclose having been exposed, which could drive cases underground, and cause the virus to spread even more."

Jeremy Konyndyk, president of Refugees International and former leader of USAID's Ebola response, expressed similar concerns about recruitment. "That's basically telling any American health worker who might go and work on the effort to contain this outbreak that if they get sick, they can't come home," he said. "It disincentivizes people from going."

Konyndyk noted that during the 2014-2015 outbreak, officials avoided travel restrictions specifically because they understood such measures would undermine containment efforts.

The U.S. has also implemented broader travel restrictions related to the outbreak, banning green card holders who recently traveled to the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and South Sudan from returning home. Other recent travelers to these countries are also barred from entering the U.S.

Experts emphasize that transportation risks are minimal for people without symptoms, and the U.S. has extensive experience evacuating exposed individuals.

cards.headline: Supreme Court Rules Death Row Inmate Can Challenge Racial Bias in Jury Selection
cards.teaser: The court sided with a Black Mississippi death row inmate who alleged prosecutors excluded Black jurors from his trial because of their race.
cards.body:
The Supreme Court ruled that a Mississippi death row inmate can proceed with his challenge to jury selection in his case, allowing him to pursue claims of racial discrimination by prosecutors. The decision enables him to contest the removal of Black jurors from his trial.

Justices Brett Kavanaugh and John Roberts joined the majority in upholding the inmate's right to challenge the exclusion of Black potential jurors. The case addresses allegations that prosecutors systematically removed Black jurors, potentially violating constitutional protections against racial discrimination in jury selection.

cards.headline: Guatemala agrees to joint anti-drug operations with U.S. inside its borders
cards.teaser: The Central American country became the latest to accept joint strikes against drug gangs as part of the Trump administration's regional campaign.
cards.body:
Guatemala agreed to allow joint operations with U.S. forces against drug trafficking organizations inside Guatemalan territory. The deal is part of a broader Trump administration effort to secure agreements with Latin American countries for cross-border anti-gang operations.

The agreement expands the administration's campaign to conduct joint military or law enforcement strikes in partner countries. Several Latin American nations have faced pressure from Washington to accept such arrangements as a condition for continued cooperation or aid.

cards.headline: Senate Republicans Rally Behind Ken Paxton Despite Concerns
cards.teaser: Republican senators are supporting Ken Paxton following his primary victory over John Cornyn, though the outcome has raised financial worries for the party.
cards.body:
Senate Republicans have consolidated support behind Ken Paxton after his win in the Texas Republican primary. Paxton defeated incumbent John Cornyn, reshaping the race and creating what some describe as a $250 million funding gap in Trump's Senate map.

The outcome of the Paxton-Talarico general election race could have significant implications for Republican Senate control. Party officials are now confronting potential money problems in Texas, a state that has required less financial investment in recent cycles.

cards.headline: Israel cuts diplomatic ties with UN chief over sexual violence blacklist
cards.teaser: Israel announced it will sever relations with the UN secretary general after being added to a list of parties committing sexual violence.
cards.body:
Israel announced it will sever ties with UN Secretary General António Guterres after the organization added Israel to a blacklist of parties accused of committing sexual violence. The decision marks a significant deterioration in relations between Israel and the UN's top official.

In a letter to Israel, Guterres cited an increasing number of allegations of sexual violence against Palestinian detainees. The blacklist typically includes armed groups and governments accused of systematic sexual violence in conflict zones.

cards.headline: Austrian man sentenced to 15 years for planning attack on Taylor Swift concert
cards.teaser: A 21-year-old was convicted of plotting a terrorist attack at a Vienna concert venue where Taylor Swift was scheduled to perform.
cards.body:
A 21-year-old Austrian man has been convicted and sentenced to 15 years in prison for planning a terrorist attack at a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna. He was also found guilty of additional terrorism-related offenses.

The plot was discovered and stopped before it could be executed, leading authorities to cancel the scheduled concerts.

cards.headline: Israel strikes Beirut in first attack on Lebanese capital during current conflict
cards.teaser: Israel conducted what it called a targeted strike in Beirut, breaking an informal understanding that had spared the Lebanese capital.
cards.body:
Israel carried out a targeted strike on Beirut, marking the first direct attack on the Lebanese capital during the current conflict. The strike comes as both Israel and Hezbollah have traded accusations of violating last month's ceasefire agreement.

Until this attack, Beirut had been largely spared from Israeli strikes despite ongoing fighting in other parts of Lebanon.

cards.teaser: The Central American country became the latest to accept joint strikes against drug gangs as part of the Trump administration's regional campaign.
cards.body:

cards.headline: Justice Department opens criminal probe into Trump accuser E. Jean Carroll
cards.teaser: Federal prosecutors are investigating whether the former columnist lied about funding she received for her civil lawsuit against President Trump.
cards.body:
The U.S. Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into E. Jean Carroll, the former columnist who won civil cases against President Trump. The investigation focuses on whether Carroll made false statements regarding the funding sources for her civil lawsuits against Trump.

Carroll previously obtained civil verdicts against Trump in cases related to defamation and sexual abuse allegations. The criminal probe marks a new development in their ongoing legal dispute.

cards.headline: Justice Department Opens Criminal Investigation Into Nonprofit That Funded E. Jean Carroll's Legal Case
cards.teaser: Federal prosecutors are investigating a Democratic-allied nonprofit organization that helped pay legal expenses for E. Jean Carroll in her lawsuit against former President Trump.
cards.body:
The Justice Department has launched a criminal investigation into a nonprofit organization that helped finance E. Jean Carroll's legal bills during her civil lawsuit against Donald Trump. The probe examines whether Carroll made false statements about the funding she received for the case.

Carroll won her civil defamation and sexual abuse lawsuit against Trump in court. The investigation focuses on the nonprofit's role in supporting her legal costs, with federal prosecutors examining the details of this financial arrangement.

cards.headline: U.S. and Iran Reach Tentative Agreement to Extend Ceasefire
cards.teaser: American and Iranian officials say they have reached a preliminary deal to extend their ceasefire, though Tehran has sent conflicting signals about the agreement.
cards.body:
U.S. officials have announced that American and Iranian negotiators have reached a tentative agreement to extend the current ceasefire. The deal reportedly includes reopening the Strait of Hormuz and would extend the truce for 60 days, pending final approval from President Trump.

However, accounts from Tehran differ significantly. Iranian news agencies have reported that no agreement has been finalized or confirmed by Iranian authorities, creating conflicting narratives about the status of negotiations between the two nations.

cards.headline: Treasury Department Plans New $250 Bill Featuring Trump's Portrait
cards.teaser: The Treasury Department is preparing to introduce a $250 denomination bill that would feature President Trump's image, though congressional approval is required.
cards.body:
The White House is pushing Congress to approve a $250 banknote bearing President Trump's portrait. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the bill would commemorate the country's 250th anniversary of independence, and confirmed the Treasury has begun preparing for the new currency.

Federal law currently prohibits printing images of living people on U.S. currency, so Congress would need to pass legislation to make an exception. Democrats have vowed to block the measure, while Trump allies in Congress support the move.

cards.teaser: A Vienna court convicted a 21-year-old man of plotting to attack a Taylor Swift concert and other terrorism offenses.
cards.body:
A 21-year-old Austrian man has been sentenced to 15 years in prison after being found guilty of planning an attack on a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna. He was also convicted of additional terrorism-related offences.

The plot was prevented before it could be executed.

hero.headline: Anthropic Valuation Reaches $965 Billion, Surpassing OpenAI
hero.body:
Anthropic raised $65 billion in a Series H funding round that valued the artificial intelligence company at $965 billion, making it the most valuable AI startup in the world. The valuation exceeds that of rival OpenAI.

The funding round represents a sharp increase in the company's market value. Anthropic develops AI models and tools that compete directly with OpenAI's products in the generative AI market.

The $965 billion post-money valuation places Anthropic among the most valuable private technology companies globally. The company has attracted significant investor interest as businesses and consumers adopt AI tools at a rapid pace.

Anthropic's rise reflects the broader surge in AI investment and development. The company's products include Claude, an AI assistant that competes with OpenAI's ChatGPT and other conversational AI tools.

The funding comes as AI companies race to develop more capable models and expand their market share. Anthropic and OpenAI have emerged as the leading players in the generative AI space, attracting billions in investment from venture capital firms and technology giants.

The near-trillion-dollar valuation marks a significant milestone for Anthropic, which was founded more recently than OpenAI but has quickly gained ground in the competitive AI market. The company's rapid ascent demonstrates investor confidence in its technology and business model.

Neither Anthropic nor its investors disclosed the specific terms of the funding round beyond the valuation figure. The round underscores the high stakes in the AI sector, where companies are competing for dominance in what many investors view as a transformative technology market.

cards.headline: Dell Revenue Growth Accelerates on AI Server Sales
cards.teaser: Dell Technologies reported its fastest sales growth since returning to public markets in 2018, driven by artificial intelligence server demand.
cards.body:
Dell Technologies shares jumped 19 percent after the company reported first quarter results that exceeded analyst estimates. The server maker posted its fastest revenue growth since becoming a public company again in 2018, propelled by sales of AI infrastructure.

The company raised its outlook for AI server sales to $60 billion for the year. Dell reported quarterly results and guidance that topped Wall Street expectations across key metrics, with artificial intelligence products driving the performance.

cards.headline: Stock Indexes Close at Record Highs as Iran Ceasefire Extended
cards.teaser: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq reached new closing records as investors reacted to reports that the United States and Iran agreed to extend a ceasefire.
cards.body:
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq reached record closing levels, with technology stocks driving the broader market advance. The rally followed reports of a tentative ceasefire extension agreement between the US and Iran, though officials in Tehran provided conflicting information about whether a deal had been finalized.

Oil prices initially rose amid conflict concerns but later retreated as investors responded to ceasefire hopes. The market's climb to new highs came despite underlying economic headwinds, including inflation rising at its fastest pace in three years in April, driven partly by higher energy prices from the Iran conflict.

cards.headline: Google Engineer Charged With Using Internal Data for Polymarket Bets
cards.teaser: Federal prosecutors charged a Google employee with using confidential company search data to win $1.2 million on the prediction market platform Polymarket.
cards.body:
The US Department of Justice has charged Michele Spagnuolo, a 36-year-old Google software engineer, with using insider information to place bets on Polymarket. Prosecutors allege he leveraged confidential Google search data to make winning predictions about the platform's markets, earning $1.2 million in profits.

Spagnuolo's arrest marks another insider trading case involving prediction markets. It comes shortly after federal prosecutors charged a US Army soldier with using classified information to place Polymarket bets about military operations.

cards.headline: Costco Revenue Exceeds Expectations With 11 Percent Sales Jump
cards.teaser: Costco reported quarterly revenue that topped Wall Street forecasts, with sales climbing 11 percent from the prior year period.
cards.body:
Costco posted sales growth that exceeded analyst expectations in its latest quarterly results. The warehouse retailer reported an 11 percent increase in sales, beating Wall Street revenue projections.

The company's earnings and membership numbers fell short of some analyst estimates despite the strong sales performance. Costco shares did not participate in a broader rally among retail stocks following the mixed quarterly report.

cards.headline: Federal Regulator Pauses Review of Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern Merger
cards.teaser: The Surface Transportation Board delayed proceedings on the $85 billion merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern, requesting additional information.
cards.body:
The Surface Transportation Board conditionally accepted the revised merger application from Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern but paused its review. The regulator requested more data from the two railroad companies before proceeding with its evaluation of the $85 billion combination.

Union Pacific disputed new claims raised during the application process, stating it had provided complete answers in its merger paperwork. The STB's decision to delay the proceedings introduces uncertainty into the timeline for combining the two railroad giants.

cards.headline: ABC Files Station License Renewals Under Protest, Cites Free Speech Concerns
cards.teaser: Disney's ABC network submitted broadcast license renewals to the FCC under protest, accusing the commission of unconstitutional retaliation.
cards.body:
ABC told the Federal Communications Commission that an early review of its broadcast licenses threatens free speech. The network filed renewal applications for its television stations under protest after the FCC moved up the expiration date to May 28.

Disney's ABC accused the FCC of unconstitutional retaliation in the station license dispute. The network argued that Americans bear the cost of the commission's order requiring early license renewals.

hero.headline: Anthropic raises $65 billion at $965 billion valuation ahead of planned IPO
hero.body:
Anthropic has closed a $65 billion Series H funding round, valuing the artificial intelligence startup at $965 billion after the investment. The company disclosed that this could be its final private fundraise before a public stock offering.

The valuation positions Anthropic among the most valuable private technology companies globally. The funding round represents one of the largest private capital raises in the technology sector.

Anthropric develops large language models and AI systems. The company has raised multiple funding rounds as it builds and deploys its technology products.

The Series H round brings Anthropic close to a $1 trillion valuation threshold. The company indicated that an initial public offering is under consideration following this fundraise.

The capital will support continued development of Anthropic's AI systems and business operations. The company competes in a rapidly expanding market for large language model technology.

Investor interest in AI companies has driven significant capital into the sector over the past several years. Anthropic's valuation reflects expectations about the commercial potential of advanced AI systems.

The company has not announced a specific timeline for a potential IPO. Going public would allow broader investor access to Anthropic shares and provide additional capital for expansion.

The funding environment for AI startups has remained active despite broader technology market conditions. Anthropic's ability to raise at this valuation demonstrates continued investor appetite for companies developing foundational AI technology.

The Series H round concludes a sequence of private fundraising that has positioned Anthropic as one of the most heavily capitalized AI companies. The path from this round to public markets will determine how investors outside the private funding ecosystem value the company's technology and business model.

cards.headline: FBI says Google engineer used internal search data to win $1.2 million on Polymarket
cards.teaser: Federal investigators say a Google employee used advance knowledge of bet outcomes to profit on a prediction market.
cards.body:
The US Justice Department has charged Michele Spagnuolo, a 36-year-old Google software engineer, with using insider information to place bets on Polymarket. Spagnuolo allegedly leveraged access to data about Google's most-searched terms to make informed wagers on the prediction market platform, earning $1.2 million in profits.

The case is part of a broader pattern of insider trading allegations involving prediction markets. Last month, prosecutors charged a US Army soldier with using classified information to place bets on Polymarket regarding military operations in Venezuela.

cards.headline: Hackers target Signal users with phishing attacks to steal backup access
cards.teaser: A new campaign attempts to trick Signal users into revealing secret recovery keys for online message backups.
cards.body:
A new phishing campaign is attempting to trick Signal users into revealing their secret recovery keys. These keys grant access to online backups that store past messages on the encrypted messaging platform.

By obtaining a user's recovery key, attackers could access the backed-up conversations stored in Signal's system. The campaign represents a targeted effort to compromise the security of Signal's backup infrastructure.

cards.headline: Cloud providers redesign infrastructure for machine-generated internet traffic
cards.teaser: AWS, Cloudflare and other companies are rebuilding systems to handle AI agents rather than human users.
cards.body:
Major cloud infrastructure providers including AWS and Cloudflare are redesigning their systems as AI agents transition from experimental projects to production environments. This shift reflects a fundamental change in how internet traffic is expected to flow, with machines increasingly generating the majority of online activity rather than human users.

The infrastructure changes account for the different patterns and demands that machine-generated traffic creates compared to traditional human internet usage. Cloud companies are adapting their platforms to handle this transition as automated systems become more prevalent in production systems.

cards.headline: Fine-tuned language models present false statements as true despite warnings
cards.teaser: Tests show AI models display bias toward confidently representing claims as accurate even after being told they are false.
cards.body:
Language models continue to assert false statements as true even after receiving explicit warnings about their inaccuracy, according to fine-tuning tests. Researchers found bias in the models toward confidently representing claims as true.

The testing examined how large language models handle information they are specifically told is false. The results showed the systems maintained tendencies to present the false claims as accurate in their outputs.

cards.headline: Developer adds hidden prompt injection to delete AI-generated code output
cards.teaser: A programmer inserted an undisclosed instruction in jqwik that told AI coding agents to erase application output.
cards.body:
A developer added a concealed prompt injection into their code that instructed AI coding agents to delete app output. The addition was placed in jqwik without disclosure to users.

The injection targeted what the developer termed vibe coders, those using AI tools to generate code. The hidden instruction told AI agents to remove the application's output when processing the code.

cards.headline: Asana acquires no-code AI agent builder StackAI
cards.teaser: The work management platform will integrate StackAI into its AI workflow tools.
cards.body:
Asana has acquired StackAI, a platform for building AI agents without coding. The company plans to incorporate StackAI into its expanding collection of AI workflow tools.

StackAI allows users to create automated AI agents through a no-code interface. Asana's acquisition adds this capability to its work management platform as it builds out AI-powered features.

hero.headline: Four-time Stanley Cup champion Claude Lemieux dies at 60
hero.body:
Claude Lemieux, a four-time Stanley Cup champion known for his intense and physical approach to playoff hockey, has died at age 60. The NHL Alumni Association announced his death on social media.

Lemieux won Stanley Cups with three different franchises during his professional career. He captured championships with the Montreal Canadiens, the New Jersey Devils twice, and the Colorado Avalanche. His reputation as a fierce competitor made him one of the most intimidating players during the postseason.

The right winger had a 21-season NHL career, playing in more than 1,200 regular season games. He scored 379 goals and recorded 406 assists during his time in the league. His postseason record was particularly impressive, with 80 goals across 234 playoff games.

In 1995, Lemieux won the Conn Smythe Trophy as playoff MVP when the New Jersey Devils won their first Stanley Cup. That year, he scored 13 goals during the postseason, helping the Devils defeat the heavily favored Detroit Red Wings in the finals.

Lemieux's playing style was often controversial. He was involved in several notable playoff incidents that generated strong reactions from opponents. One such incident was a hit on Detroit's Kris Draper in 1996, which sparked a prolonged rivalry between the Colorado Avalanche and Detroit Red Wings. While his aggressive approach sometimes created animosity with opposing players, his teammates appreciated his commitment to winning.

After his playing career ended, Lemieux remained involved in professional hockey. He worked in player development and coaching roles at various levels of the sport. He was also the father of Brendan Lemieux, who played in the NHL for multiple teams including the Winnipeg Jets and New York Rangers.

Lemieux also worked as a player agent, continuing his involvement with hockey after leaving the game as a competitor.

The hockey community responded to his death with numerous tributes. Former teammates and opponents acknowledged both his exceptional skill and his competitive intensity. Many highlighted how Lemieux consistently elevated his performance when stakes were highest, establishing himself as one of the most productive playoff performers in hockey history.

His four Stanley Cup championships placed him among an elite group of players who won multiple titles with different organizations. His legacy in professional hockey remains defined by his fierce determination and postseason success across his long career in the sport.

cards.headline: MLB proposes hard salary cap in opening collective bargaining offer
cards.teaser: Major League Baseball submitted its first proposal to the players union, including details of a hard salary cap for the first time since the 1994 strike.
cards.body:
Major League Baseball owners presented their opening collective bargaining proposal to the players union, which includes a hard salary cap—the first such proposal since the 1994 player strike that led to the cancellation of the World Series. The proposal establishes a salary floor of $171 million, setting both minimum and maximum payroll levels for teams.

The league framed the proposal as a means to address competitive balance concerns across baseball's 30 franchises.

cards.headline: NBA approves new draft lottery system to reduce tanking incentive
cards.teaser: The NBA Board of Governors voted to expand the draft lottery and change odds distribution, aiming to discourage teams from deliberately losing games.
cards.body:
The NBA Board of Governors approved changes to the draft lottery system designed to address tanking. The new system expands the lottery beyond the current format and adjusts the odds of receiving top picks.

Under the revised structure, the worst teams no longer have the best odds of landing the top draft selection. The changes aim to reduce the incentive for teams to deliberately lose games to improve draft position.

cards.headline: World number one Jannik Sinner loses in French Open second round
cards.teaser: Top seed Jannik Sinner fell to Juan Manuel Cerundolo in one of the biggest upsets in recent French Open history, saying he lacked energy during the match.
cards.body:
Jannik Sinner, the world number one, suffered a shock second-round exit at the French Open, losing to Argentina's Juan Manuel Cerúndolo 3-6, 2-6, 7-5, 6-1, 6-1. Sinner attributed his poor performance to illness rather than the extreme Paris heat, saying he lacked energy throughout the match.

The Italian described the defeat as tough to accept given his recent form and ranking. He plans to skip grass-court tournaments and take time to recover both physically and mentally before preparing for Wimbledon.

cards.headline: Connecticut Sun waive Hailey Van Lith for second time this month
cards.teaser: The Sun released second-year guard Hailey Van Lith after nine games, marking her second waiver in May, and activated guard Leila Lacan.
cards.body:
The Connecticut Sun waived guard Hailey Van Lith, a 2025 first-round draft pick, after she appeared in just nine games for the team. This marks the second time Van Lith has been waived in May.

The Sun activated guard Leila Lacan to fill the roster spot. Van Lith, who played one season in the WNBA, now faces an uncertain future as she searches for her third team in less than a month.

cards.headline: Luke Littler beats Luke Humphries to win Premier League Darts title
cards.teaser: World champion Luke Littler defeated Luke Humphries 11-10 in one of the greatest Premier League Darts finals to regain the title.
cards.body:
World champion Luke Littler delivered one of his finest performances to claim revenge over Luke Humphries in the Premier League final. Littler secured an 11-10 victory in a thrilling match that ranks among the competition's greatest finals.

The closely fought contest came down to the final leg, with Littler ultimately prevailing to regain the Premier League title.

cards.headline: Serena Williams in talks for return to tennis at Queen's Club
cards.teaser: Serena Williams is discussing a potential comeback to competitive tennis at the Queen's Club tournament next month.
cards.body:
Serena Williams is considering a comeback to competitive tennis at Queen's Club in London, beginning June 8. The 23-time Grand Slam champion, who last competed in 2022, would be 44 years old at the time of her return.

Williams has been cleared to compete after re-entering the professional drug-testing pool six months ago. She is reportedly seeking a doubles wildcard at the Queen's WTA 500 event, partnering with Canadian Victoria Mboko, the 19-year-old ranked No. 19 in singles.

hero.headline: Austrian Man Sentenced to 15 Years for Plot to Attack Taylor Swift Vienna Concert
hero.body:
A 21-year-old Austrian man has been sentenced to 15 years in prison after being found guilty of planning a jihadist attack on Taylor Swift's Vienna concerts in 2024. The defendant, identified as Beran A under Austrian privacy laws, pleaded guilty to terrorism-related charges connected to the foiled plot.

The planned attack targeted concertgoers at Ernst Happel stadium during Swift's Eras Tour performances scheduled for August 2024. Authorities discovered that Beran A intended to use knives or homemade explosives to target up to 30,000 people gathered outside the venue, plus another 65,000 inside. Prosecutors said he hoped to "kill as many people as possible."

Austrian authorities discovered bomb-making materials during a search of his apartment on August 7, 2024, just one day before the concerts were scheduled to begin. The discovery led officials to cancel all three Vienna performances. Swift later posted on Instagram about the cancellation, saying "The reason for the cancellations filled me with a new sense of fear, and a tremendous amount of guilt because so many people had planned on coming to those shows."

During questioning at trial, Beran A said "Yes" when asked whether he pleaded guilty to charges linked to the planned concert attack. His defense attorney, Anna Mair, stated that her client "deeply regrets it all" and described his actions as "the biggest mistake of his life." Beran A has been in custody since his arrest in August 2024.

The charges against him include terrorist offences and membership in a terrorist organization. Prosecutors alleged that Beran A shared Islamic State propaganda through messaging services and openly aligned himself with IS. He allegedly sought to illegally purchase weapons including a machine gun and hand grenade, and used IS video instructions to produce a small amount of the explosive triacetone triperoxide.

Beyond the Swift concert plot, Beran A and another man, Slovak national Arda K, were accused of planning attacks in the Middle East during Ramadan 2024. A third man, Hasan E, is suspected of carrying out a knife attack in Mecca on March 11, 2024. Both Beran A and Arda K pleaded guilty to traveling to their designated cities with intentions to carry out militant attacks but pleaded not guilty to providing moral support to Hasan E.

The trial took place in Wiener Neustadt, about an hour south of Vienna. U.S. intelligence contributed to the decision to cancel the concerts. The case drew international comparisons to the 2017 Manchester bombing at an Ariana Grande concert, which killed 22 people. A Berlin court previously convicted a Syrian teenager of contributing to the Swift concert plot, sentencing him to an 18-month suspended sentence.

cards.headline: Google Employee Allegedly Used Insider Data to Win $1.2 Million in Online Bet
cards.teaser: Federal authorities say a Google staffer used confidential search data to profit from Polymarket trades predicting D4vd would be the most searched term of 2025.
cards.body:
A Google software engineer has been charged with using insider information to profit from prediction market bets. Michele Spagnuolo, 36, allegedly earned $1.2 million through trades on Polymarket by accessing confidential data about Google's most-searched terms that wasn't available to the public.

The Italian citizen's arrest follows a similar case involving a US Army soldier charged with using classified information to place bets on the same platform. Spagnuolo allegedly wagered on long-shot candidates, leveraging his access to internal search trend data for financial gain.

cards.headline: ABC Challenges FCC License Renewal Order as Unconstitutional
cards.teaser: Disney's ABC submitted broadcast license renewal applications for its eight TV stations under protest, calling the FCC order unlawful and arbitrary.
cards.body:
Disney's ABC submitted license renewal applications for its eight owned-and-operated television stations to the Federal Communications Commission while formally objecting to the process. The network filed the applications under protest.

The FCC's Media Bureau issued an order requiring ABC to reapply for spectrum licenses for its local stations. ABC characterized the bureau's order as unprecedented, unlawful, arbitrary and unconstitutional.

cards.headline: Nick Bilton Takes Over 60 Minutes, Aims for Broader Digital Presence
cards.teaser: The new executive producer wants the newsmagazine to extend beyond its traditional Sunday evening slot on CBS.
cards.body:
CBS News appointed Nick Bilton, a former New York Times tech journalist, as executive producer of 60 Minutes, replacing Tanya Simon. The leadership change comes as part of broader shifts at the newsmagazine ahead of its 59th season in the fall.

Bilton's appointment signals CBS News' intent to modernize the long-running Sunday program. As executive producer, he will oversee the show's direction and content strategy moving forward.

cards.headline: Scooter Braun Discusses Taylor Swift, Kanye West in Rare Interview
cards.teaser: The retired music manager sat for a 90-minute conversation on the Second Thought podcast, his first extensive interview since leaving management.
cards.body:
Scooter Braun sat down for a 90-minute interview on the Second Thought podcast with Suzy Weiss, where he discussed his relationships with Taylor Swift, Kanye West, Spencer Pratt and Sydney Sweeney. The conversation marks a rare public appearance for Braun, who has stepped back from the spotlight in recent years.

Braun retired from management and left his position as CEO of Hybe America. During his career in the music industry, he managed major artists including Justin Bieber, Ariana Grande, and Kanye West. The interview represents one of his few public discussions since departing from the entertainment business.

cards.headline: Love Island USA Announces Season 8 Cast
cards.teaser: The reality show's new season includes the brother of a previous contestant and a Paralympic bronze medalist.
cards.body:
Love Island USA has unveiled 12 new cast members for Season 8. Notable contestants include Zach Georgiou, whose brother Charlie competed in Season 7, and Beatriz Hatz, a bronze medal-winning Paralympic athlete.

The season premieres June 2 with daily episodes airing throughout the first week. Following premiere week, the schedule will shift to a different format. The show will feature its villa setting with the newly selected group of contestants.

cards.headline: Robyn to Headline San Francisco's Portola Music Festival
cards.teaser: The Swedish pop star will lead the 2026 lineup alongside Dog Blood and Swedish House Mafia.
cards.body:
Robyn will headline Portola Music Festival in San Francisco in 2026. The festival announced its lineup with the Swedish artist as a main attraction.

Other headliners include Dog Blood and Swedish House Mafia. Additional performers include Zara Larsson and Four Tet. The festival released its full lineup and announced when tickets will go on sale.

hero.headline: U.S. to quarantine Americans exposed to Ebola in Kenya, barring them from returning home
hero.body:
The Trump administration confirmed this week that Americans exposed to Ebola will not be permitted to return to the United States. Instead, the government is constructing a 50-bed quarantine and treatment facility in Kenya that became operational Friday.

The White House said the facility was "designed to provide access to high-quality care for Americans who would need to quickly get out of DRC and quarantine without the risks of a lengthy transport back to the US," according to a statement from a White House official.

The Kenya center will handle both quarantine for exposed individuals and treatment for those who contract the virus. The official stated the facility would provide "critical care needs, though each case will be evaluated for forward transport for more advanced care as appropriate in order to maximize patient outcomes." The official did not specify whether additional treatment would occur in the United States or Europe, where some Americans have previously received care.

The administration also did not clarify whether Americans could choose to return to the U.S. instead of going to Kenya.

The policy has drawn criticism from public health experts. Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health, said the approach raises serious concerns.

"It is shocking to me that the administration is looking to prevent Americans from coming home to receive the proven world-class care that our taxpayer-funded biocontainment and treatment units are equipped to provide," Nuzzo said. "There are profound ethical concerns with this approach."

She worried that the policy could discourage people from reporting exposures. "Without adequate plans for the safe quarantine of exposed individuals and prompt isolation of those who become infected, I fear these facilities could amplify the spread of the virus. The prospect of not being able to come home for safe and effective care may create disincentives for people to disclose having been exposed, which could drive cases underground, and cause the virus to spread even more."

Jeremy Konyndyk, president of Refugees International and former leader of USAID's Ebola response, expressed similar concerns about recruitment. "That's basically telling any American health worker who might go and work on the effort to contain this outbreak that if they get sick, they can't come home," he said. "It disincentivizes people from going."

Konyndyk noted that during the 2014-2015 outbreak, officials avoided travel restrictions specifically because they understood such measures would undermine containment efforts.

The U.S. has also implemented broader travel restrictions related to the outbreak, banning green card holders who recently traveled to the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and South Sudan from returning home. Other recent travelers to these countries are also barred from entering the U.S.

Experts emphasize that transportation risks are minimal for people without symptoms, and the U.S. has extensive experience evacuating exposed individuals.

cards.headline: Justice Department investigating Reid Hoffman nonprofit over E. Jean Carroll case contributions
cards.teaser: The DOJ is examining the LinkedIn co-founder's nonprofit, which contributed to legal expenses for Carroll's civil lawsuit against Trump.
cards.body:
The Department of Justice has launched a criminal investigation into billionaire Reid Hoffman's nonprofit organization, which provided funding for E. Jean Carroll's legal expenses during her civil lawsuit against President Trump. The investigation focuses on whether Carroll made false statements regarding the funding she received.

Carroll, a former columnist, successfully sued Trump for sexual assault. Two juries awarded her millions of dollars in damages. Hoffman, who co-founded LinkedIn, has been a major donor to Democratic causes and a vocal critic of Trump.

cards.headline: Treasury Secretary Bessent dismisses question about 2028 presidential run
cards.teaser: Scott Bessent deflected when asked about presidential ambitions during a White House press briefing where he filled in for the press secretary.
cards.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dismissed a question about his presidential ambitions Thursday while filling in for press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who is on maternity leave. Bessent spoke for more than 30 minutes during the White House briefing.

Bessent discussed the Trump administration's negotiations with Iran, the impending launch of Trump Accounts for children, and other policy matters. He did not address the 2028 question directly, moving past it during the session.

cards.headline: Hakeem Jeffries opposes Trump $250 bill proposal
cards.teaser: The House Minority Leader called the reported push for a bill featuring Trump's face a hard no.
cards.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries rejected the White House push for a $250 bill featuring President Trump's portrait. Jeffries said he was a "hard no" on the proposal and told Trump to get over himself.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the bill would celebrate the nation's 250th anniversary of independence. The Treasury Department has already begun preparing designs for the currency. However, federal law currently prohibits printing images of living people on US currency, requiring Congress to pass new legislation before the bill could be produced. Democrats have pledged to block the move.

cards.headline: Court orders Customs chief to testify on tariff refunds process
cards.teaser: Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott must appear at a hearing next month about the Trump administration's tariff refund implementation.
cards.body:
The U.S. Court of International Trade ordered the commissioner for Customs and Border Protection to appear at a hearing next month to testify about the tariff refunds process being implemented by the Trump administration. The order was issued Wednesday.

Commissioner Rodney Scott has been ordered to testify at the hearing, which will take place in New York on June 9. The court is examining how the administration is handling the refund process for tariffs paid by importers and businesses.

cards.headline: Treasury Secretary disputes Washington Post report on $250 Trump banknote
cards.teaser: Scott Bessent questioned reporting about a planned commemorative bill featuring the president during a White House briefing.
cards.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent challenged a Washington Post article about a planned commemorative $250 bill featuring President Trump during a White House press briefing Thursday. Bessent expressed confusion about the reporting and disputed aspects of the Treasury Department's plans for the banknote.

The proposal has drawn criticism from Democratic leaders. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries firmly opposed the idea, telling Trump to "get over yourself." Any new currency denomination would require congressional approval before the Bureau of Engraving and Printing could begin production.

cards.headline: The View hosts criticize DOJ investigation of E. Jean Carroll
cards.teaser: The ABC talk show questioned why the administration is relitigating a case already decided by two juries.
cards.body:
The hosts of ABC's The View criticized the Trump administration on Thursday for launching a criminal investigation into E. Jean Carroll, the writer who accused President Trump of sexual assault and won her civil lawsuit against him.

The DOJ investigation focuses on whether Carroll made false statements about funding she received for her legal case. The probe also targets a nonprofit organization linked to billionaire Reid Hoffman, which contributed money that partially covered Carroll's legal expenses during the civil lawsuit.
